I write product pages for software companies, and I have one test for every sentence. I call it the so what test. Our tool has a pre-built SAP connector. So what? So you go live in days, not months. The first sentence is a feature. The second is a benefit, and the benefit is the one the customer remembers. Most engineers write pages full of features, because they built them and they are proud of them. A buyer does not care what the tool has. A buyer cares about what changes on Monday morning. The other thing I fix is adjectives. People write things like an innovative powerful new smart solution. Four adjectives, zero information. One good adjective in the right place is better than four, and a number is better than any adjective.

Before a first call with a vendor, I spend about two minutes on their product page. I skip every word that every vendor uses: innovative, world-class, next-generation. Those words tell me nothing. What I look for is three things. First, does it connect to the system we already have, and how long does that take? Second, who on my team will use it, and do they need training? And third, is there a number I can check, like how many customers or how many invoices a year? When a page answers those three questions in the first screen, I go to the call with good questions. When it does not, I go to the call with doubts, and the salesperson has to work much harder.
